newsitem.title: USA: Trains collide in Kansas, chemicals catch fire.
newsitem.headline: Trains collide in Kansas, chemicals catch fire.

text.p: Two Union Pacific freight trains collided in eastern Kansas early Wednesday, killing an engineer and threatening a chemical spill that forced 1,500 residents to evacuate, authorities said.

The engineer who was killed overshot a railroad siding and struck the oncoming train six cars back from the locomotive, derailing a total of 20 freight cars, John Bromley, a spokesman for Union Pacific Railroad in Omaha, Nebraska, said. A conductor on one of trains received minor injuries.

Sirens sounded around 3 a.m. CDT in Rossville about 4 miles south of the wreck and officers went door-to-door waking the town's 1,500 residents in the emergency evacuation. They were allowed to return about eight hours later.
A subsequent diesel fuel fire was doused by a National Guard helicopter that scooped water from a nearby lake with a giant bucket and dumped it on wreck.
Both trains carried a mixed cargo including automobiles and hazardous chemicals but it was not clear if any of the dangerous materials had spilled, Bromley said.
But Shawnee County Sheriff Dave Meneley said chlorine and sulphur dioxide, both potentially toxic chemicals, had spilled.
"Several chemicals spilled, chlorine being one of them, which is highly toxic," Meneley said. "There's a large cloud; that's the reason for the evacuation."

Bromley said the eastbound train that was struck was hauling 42 freight cars including an empty chlorine tank car. The wreck occurred about 14 miles northwest of Topeka and a spokesman for Kansas Gov. Bill Graves said the governor could see the cloud of smoke from his home on the northwest edge of the city. He joined local officials overseeing the evacuation.

It was the second fatal train wreck in less than two weeks involving Union Pacific trains. Federal authorities have been investigating the June 22 head-on collision of two freight trains in Devine, Texas, that killed four people and triggered a fiery explosion of thousands of gallons of diesel fuel.
News reports said investigators believe a Union Pacific dispatcher's error led to that wreck.
In another incident, a Union Pacific dispatcher sent a coal train into the path of a suburban Chicago commuter train last week, but the trains stopped two miles apart.
"It's unusual to have two major accidents like this within a very short time, and we're looking at whether it's a systematic problem," Bromley said.
